newsitem.title: FRANCE: French bank siege grinds into sixth day.
newsitem.headline: French bank siege grinds into sixth day.

text.p: A siege at the headquarters of property lending group Credit Foncier dragged into a sixth day on Wednesday as staff holding top executives hostage poured cold water on a mediator's plan to break the deadlock.

Staff assembled in the bank's giant atrium were due to vote on Wednesday on a proposal by government-appointed mediator Philippe Rouvillois to put plans to dismantle the bank on hold while negotiations with staff continued, union officials said.
But staff representatves said protestors were ready to dig in their heels and keep the siege going if they did not get better guarantees over the fate of around 1,000 jobs.
"The proposals we have been given are too vague. We are seeking stronger assurances," one union official said.

Bank chairman Jerome Meyssonnier and seven of his colleagues have been held in the bank offices since Friday in a protest over a plan by the government to split up the group, which it saved from bankruptcy last year.

Unions say the proposal to spin off its main commercial activities, including low-cost social housing loans, to a cooperatively run credit group called Credit Immobilier threatens nearly a third of the bank's 3,300 jobs.
Staff want more time to try to find a rescue partner prepared to keep the 145-year-old lender alive in one piece.

Pressure on the government to clarify the bank's position increased on Wednesday when a senior European Union official said that Brussels was waiting for details of the French government's financing strategy within less than two weeks.

Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert told French business daily La Tribune the EU Commission had been studying the financing of Credit Foncier since last year and that Paris had promised to deliver a concrete plan by the end of January.

The French government rescued Credit Foncier from collapse with a state-orchestrated takeover last year and now wants to press on with the next stage of its project -- spinning off the core business to Credit Immobilier and winding down the rest.
Credit Foncier says it is making money on its basic activities after a massive 11 billion franc ($2.01 billion) loss in 1995, but its balance sheet is at least three billion francs in the red.
